text: Our dad died and left the house in his will. My sister A wants to buy it with her husband at a "family discount". I'm not signing off on that. Our younger sister B could use some money too. Can you help us sort this out?

I am sorry for your loss. I can help the three of you talk through options, but I cannot make legal decisions or move money. Before anyone signs anything, I suggest we gather the will terms, who the executor is, what the house is worth, and what each sister needs. Please tell me what the will says about who inherits the house, who the executor is, what price and terms A has proposed, and what outcome would seem fair to you. I also have a process concern: no one should be pressed to sign until the facts and choices are clear, and I need us to use one shared list of needs, concerns, and expectations. I will check that with A and B.

I don’t know the will terms, executor, or A’s proposed price and terms yet. I want a fair financial share, and I haven’t agreed to subsidize a discounted purchase by A. We should settle it once the facts are clear; there’s no need to rush.

I am sorry for your loss. C contacted me to help the three of you discuss the house. I cannot make legal decisions or move money. I will keep a shared list and not take sides. Please tell me what you and your husband propose, including price, timing, who would own it, and whether the offer would include everyone with a legal interest under the will. Also say what you need from this process and any deadlines you face. Please share what you know about the will, the executor, and any debts or costs tied to the house. My process concern is that no one should be pressed to sign until the facts and choices are clear; I will check that with everyone.

My husband and I would like to buy the house at a family discount, but we haven’t set a price, timing, or ownership details. C’s agreement is needed. I don’t know the will’s terms, who the executor is, or whether there are debts or costs, and I have no deadline. I’d like the facts and everyone’s options to be clear before anyone signs.

I am sorry for your loss. C contacted me to help the three of you talk through the house. I cannot make legal decisions or move money. I will keep a shared list and not take sides. C mentioned you may want money, but I want to hear from you directly. Please tell me what you need most: a quick cash share, a fair long-term share, continued family use of the house, or something else. Also tell me what you know about the will, the executor, and any proposed sale to A and her husband. My process concern is that no one should be pressed to sign until the facts and choices are clear; I will check that with everyone.

Thank you. A share of money would help me start a dance studio, so a timely cash share is probably what I need most. I don’t know the will or who the executor is; I understand A wants to buy the house, and C hasn’t agreed.

Here is the shared needs, concerns, and expectations (NCEs) list I have so far. Please tell me any line you disagree with, want changed, or want added. I have written it in the third person so all three copies match. I am sending the same list to A and B, and I will send any changes to all three. I will not treat silence or a slow reply as agreement, and I will wait for all three before using the list to weigh a draft plan.

C needs a fair financial share, does not agree to subsidize a discounted purchase by A, and wants the facts clear before any settlement.

A and her husband want to buy the house at a family discount. No price, timing, or ownership details are set. A says C's agreement is needed, has no deadline, and wants the facts and options clear before anyone signs.

B needs a timely cash share to start a dance studio and does not know the will or the executor.

All three need the will terms, the executor, any debts or costs, and one independent appraisal before choosing an option.

My own NCE is on the same list, not above it: no one signs or is pressed to sign until those facts are clear, each sister can get her own professional advice, and the shared list stays open to correction. I do not agree with treating a family discount as settled before the will, costs, and appraisal are known and everyone named in the will freely agrees. I also disagree with any plan that leaves B's timing need unanswered. Please tell me if you disagree with my line too.

Please also tell me who has the will or probate papers, the executor's name and contact, and any known debts, taxes, repairs, or mortgage. If no one has the papers, please say who will ask the executor or the probate court for a copy. Say whether you would accept one independent appraisal as a shared starting point. I cannot give legal or financial advice, make legal decisions, hire the appraiser, or move money. I can help you compare options, not choose them. Please reply with agree, change, or add.

The draft process plan has four steps. First, A offered to help find out who to contact for the will or probate papers. I suggest the sisters ask the court handling the will, Dad's lawyer, or Dad's papers for the executor's contact, and ask the executor what the will says and what the executor may do. If any sister objects to A taking the first step, say so; if someone prefers another person, say so. Because A and C are twins and B is younger, please ask whether the will uses age, birth order, or twin status. Do not guess.

Second, the sisters or the executor should choose one independent appraiser. Each sister can get her own advice and, if she wants, a second valuation. One appraisal does not set the price. I cannot choose or hire the appraiser. The executor or the sisters should also list debts, taxes, repairs, mortgage, fees, and appraisal costs before anyone compares choices.

Third, after the facts are clear, the sisters compare three choices. One choice is an open-market sale that splits net proceeds according to the will and legal advice. This meets C's no-subsidy line and may give B cash, but it may not meet A's wish to buy. Another choice is a buyout by A and her husband at a price based on the appraisal or another price all legal owners freely accept. It would need proof of funds, written terms, ownership details, a closing date, and clear treatment of debts, taxes, repairs, mortgage, fees, and appraisal costs. If A still wants a discount, she should state the amount and what each sister receives in return. Family ties alone do not answer C's no-subsidy line, and C can say no. A third choice is to ask the executor and each sister's own adviser whether a lawful early cash payment, a payment in stages, or another short-term way to get B cash sooner is possible. No private loan or advance should happen without legal advice and a written agreement. This may meet B's timing need, but I need B's target date or amount to test it.

Fourth, no one signs until all people with a legal interest under the will agree after advice, and all three sisters have had time to review. If any sister says no, that choice is not agreed. If all three agree, this is a working process plan, not a legal settlement. It does not decide who gets the house or how much anyone receives. I will not use this draft as a final plan until all three reply.

I weighed this draft against the list. The fact-finding step answers the NCEs about the will, executor, costs, and legal interests. The appraisal step answers A's clarification and C's fairness concern, but it does not set price. The sale and buyout choices answer C's fair share line, A's wish, and B's cash need in different ways. The short-term cash choice may answer B's timing need, but it could fail C's no-rush and no-subsidy lines if it creates pressure.

I disagree with treating a family discount as settled before the will, costs, appraisal, and free agreement by all legal owners. I disagree with treating the appraisal as the price. I disagree with assuming C's agreement is legally required, with assuming equal shares, and with any plan that leaves B's timing need unanswered. I also disagree with any plan that uses my no-pressure line to delay B indefinitely. Please tell me where you think I am wrong, including about my own NCEs or my weighing. I will not defend the list; I will change it after all three have a chance to comment.

Ask the executor and each sister's own legal adviser what the will says about each person's interests. Do not guess.

Second, the sisters or the executor should choose one independent appraiser. Each sister can get her own advice and, if she wants, a second valuation. One appraisal does not set the price. I cannot choose or hire the appraiser. No appraisal or other cost is incurred until the executor or the sisters agree in writing who pays and how much, subject to legal advice. The executor or the sisters should also list debts, taxes, repairs, mortgage, fees, and appraisal costs before anyone compares choices.

Third, after the facts are clear, the sisters compare three choices. One choice is an open-market sale that splits net proceeds according to the will and legal advice. This meets C's no-subsidy line and may give B cash, but it may not meet A's wish to buy. Another choice is a buyout by A and her husband at a price based on the appraisal or another price that the people whose consent is legally required freely accept after independent legal advice. It would need proof of funds, written terms, ownership details, a closing date, and clear treatment of debts, taxes, repairs, mortgage, fees, and appraisal costs. If A still wants a discount, she should state the amount and what each sister receives in return. Family ties alone do not answer C's no-subsidy line, and C can say no. A third choice is to ask the executor and each sister's own adviser whether a lawful early cash payment, a payment in stages, or another short-term way to get B cash sooner is possible. No private loan or advance should happen without legal advice and a written agreement. This may meet B's timing need, but it cannot be tested until B gives a target date or amount after the facts are clear.

Fourth, no one signs until independent legal advice confirms who must consent, those people agree after advice, and all three sisters have had time to review. If any sister says no, we will not call it a family agreement; legal rights are separate and must be confirmed by independent legal advice. If all three agree, this is a working process plan, not a legal settlement. It does not decide who gets the house or how much anyone receives. I will not use this draft as a final plan until all three reply.
